title: Features of Complexity, Emergence
author: Nick Hart
summary: This short entry in Hart's complexity series isolates emergence as the feature that most changes a leader's job. Order in complex systems is described as arising not only from formal authority but from the bottom up, sideways and diagonally, through patterns that form as people, routines and ideas interact. No individual designs it; coherence takes shape through many small exchanges, and innovations spread because they work rather than because they were mandated. Hart illustrates this with a thought experiment in which teachers share a frustration about marking or initiative overload, talk informally, trade ideas and run small experiments until the practice is already working by the time senior leaders notice. His point about the leader's role in that scene is the crux: not to launch the practice but to recognise it, remove barriers, lend legitimacy and avoid formalising it too soon. Four moves follow for enabling emergence, including creating conditions rather than blueprints and writing the policy only after the practice has developed. He advises attending to weak signals, the places where energy, curiosity or frustration gather, and amplifying patterns that begin to sustain themselves. The piece ends by relinquishing the illusion of control in favour of designing the conditions in which a system designs itself.
points: Hart inverts the usual sequence of school improvement by arguing that the policy should be written after the practice has developed, not before it.
The thought experiment's most useful detail is timing: by the time senior leaders notice an emergent practice, it is already working, so the leadership task is recognition rather than initiation.
Weak signals are defined operationally as the places where energy, curiosity or frustration gather, giving leaders something concrete to scan for.
Amplification is treated as a distinct leadership act, meaning making a spreading practice visible, protecting it and helping it grow once coherence appears.
The metaphor shift from pulling levers to turning dials captures the claim that leaders steward interactions rather than script outcomes.
quotes: In complex systems, order doesn’t come only from those with formal positions of authority. It also arises from the bottom up, sideways and diagonally from the patterns that form when people, routines and ideas interact.
Schools are full of such self-organising behaviours. Cultures, norms and innovations often emerge not because they were mandated, but because people found meaning and connection in them.
They trade ideas, run small experiments and share what they notice. There’s no meeting agenda or project plan, just curiosity and a shared desire to make things better.

When senior leaders finally notice, the practice is already working. Their role isn’t to launch it but to recognise it, to remove barriers, give it legitimacy and help it spread without formalising it too soon.

Focus on purpose, principles and relationships. Set the direction and the boundaries, then allow variation and adaptation. The blueprint will emerge through practice; you write the policy after the practice has developed.
Notice where energy, curiosity or frustration are gathering. These are clues to where new possibilities are forming.

Leadership in complexity means stewarding interactions, not scripting outcomes. It’s tempting to think that we can design the system but we might be better off trying to design the conditions that helps the system design itself.
